h1: Czech pale lager and German pilsner compared glass by glass
title: Czech vs German Pilsner Compared | Craft Beer School
desc: Czech pale lager and German pilsner compared: colour, malt, hops, water, bitterness and the pour, with a guide to tasting them side by side.
teaser: Same name, same pale colour, very different beers. Here is how to tell a Czech pale lager from a German pils by taste.
standfirst: Pilsner was born in the Czech town of Plzeň in 1842 and copied across Germany within decades. Today the Czech and German versions are two distinct styles. Here is what separates them and how to taste the difference.
sections:
The first golden lager was brewed in Plzeň (Pilsen in German) in 1842. It combined pale malt, soft local water, Saaz hops and bottom fermenting lager yeast. Clear glassware was becoming cheaper. A bright golden beer looked remarkable.

German brewers soon made their own versions, adapted to their own malts, hops and water. Over time the two developed into separate styles. The BJCP calls the Czech one Czech premium pale lager and the German one German pils. Our pilsner style guide covers the wider family.

Czech pale lager is deeper gold, sometimes with an amber tint. It tastes of rich bread and a light honeyed sweetness, with a fuller, rounder body. The finish is balanced and can feel slightly soft.

German pils is paler, straw to light gold. It is drier and leaner, with a clean, crackery malt flavour and a crisp, quick finish. Attenuation is higher, so less sugar is left behind.

Approximate BJCP ranges help: Czech premium pale lager is 4.2 to 5.8% ABV with 30 to 45 IBU and colour around 3.5 to 6 SRM. German pils is 4.4 to 5.2% ABV with 22 to 40 IBU and paler, around 2 to 4 SRM.

Czech pale lager uses Saaz, a noble hop with a soft, spicy, herbal and floral character. Our guide to noble hops explains the group. Bitterness is substantial but rounded, carried by the fuller malt so it never feels harsh.

German pils uses German varieties such as Hallertau, Tettnang and Spalt. The aroma is floral, herbal and a little peppery. Bitterness feels sharper and more lingering, because the leaner body offers less malt to balance it.

Plzeň water is famously soft, with very few minerals. Soft water gives a gentle bitterness even with a lot of hops. Many Czech breweries still use decoction mashing, boiling part of the mash and returning it, which deepens malt flavour and colour. Our guide to decoction mashing explains how it works.

Some German pils, especially from the north, is brewed with harder, more sulphate rich water, which sharpens bitterness and dries the finish. Infusion or step mashing is more common. Fermentation is clean, with some versions carrying a faint sulphur note from lager yeast. Czech versions may show a trace of diacetyl, which would be a fault in a German pils.

Czech pubs take pouring seriously. A hladinka has a thick, wet head of foam about a third of the glass. A šnyt is mostly foam with a little beer, for a quick taste. Mlíko is almost entirely foam, sweet and creamy, drunk fast. The dense foam softens the bitterness and protects the beer from air.

German pils is also poured with a tall, firm head, traditionally into a tall, tapered and often stemmed pilsner glass. Pouring takes time to build the foam properly.

In India, many bars pour lager very cold with little foam. That hides much of what makes either style special. Ask for a proper head if you can.

Pour both at about 6 to 8 °C into identical glasses. Look at the colour first: the Czech beer should be deeper gold. Smell: Czech beer gives bread, honey and spicy Saaz; German pils gives cracker and floral or peppery hops. Taste: notice the body. The Czech beer feels fuller. Then the finish: German pils should be drier, with bitterness that lingers longer.

Swap the order and taste again. Write down three words for each. These differences are clear once you know them, but subtle at first. Telling bread from cracker or soft bitterness from sharp is precisely the kind of discrimination that sensory training develops.

Imported Czech and German pilsners reach Indian shops, but they spend weeks in transit and often sit warm in godowns. Pale lager shows staling quickly, so an imported bottle may taste of cardboard or honey rather than fresh hops. Check the packaging date and buy from shops that keep beer cold.

A fresh pilsner from a local brewpub is often the better example, even if it is not strictly Czech or German. Ask the brewer which way they lean. Their answer about malt, hops and mash tells you what to expect in the glass.

Czech pale lager's fuller body suits fried and roasted food: pakoras, chicken 65, roast pork, pan fried fish. German pils, drier and sharper, is excellent with oily, salty food and lighter dishes: salads, fish fry, grilled prawns and anything where you want a clean palate between bites.
faqs: In Plzeň, in today's Czech Republic, in 1842.
Which is more bitter, Czech or German pilsner?
Czech pale lager often has as much or more bitterness, but its fuller malt and soft water make it feel rounder. German pils tastes sharper and drier.
The standard Czech pour, with a thick, wet head of foam about a third of the glass.
